name: freight-rate
content:
# freight-rate

- 🔗 **Repository:** https://github.com/Mishallic/freight-rate
- **Language:** Python
- **Last update:** 2026-10-05

---

Predicts the posted rate (USD) of truck loads from distance, equipment, weight, pickup and
delivery coordinates, and day of week. A LightGBM model is trained on loads from January to
October 2025 and predicts 12,000 loads from November and December 2025. It is validated
with time-based folds that each predict the two months after their training data.

## Results

MAPE on clean test rows (rows with a corrupted rate removed):

| Model | Fold A: train Jan-Jun, test Jul-Aug | Fold B: train Jan-Aug, test Sep-Oct |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline: median rate per mile by distance band and equipment | 4.00% | 3.85% |
| LightGBM, final model (V1) | 2.26% | 1.91% |

On all test rows, corrupted rates included, the final model's MAPE is 4.51% and 4.42%.
Full tables are in `reports/metrics_models.csv`; the write-up is `reports/report.md`
(also as `reports/report.docx`).

## Repository layout

```
data/                        input data, unchanged
provided/                    the supplied scorer (score.py), README and requirements, unmodified
src/
  data.py                    loading, cleaning (prepare), corrupted-rate rule
  explore.py                 data facts and figures 1-4
  evaluate.py                time-based folds, metrics, baseline model
  model.py                   features and the LightGBM model
  compare.py                 baseline vs feature variants, extra checks, figure 5
  predict.py                 final model, prediction files, scorer run, sanity checks
  report_to_docx.py          converts reports/report.md to reports/report.docx
  style.py                   shared chart colors and style
tests/                       pytest tests for cleaning, folds, metrics and features
reports/                     write-up, metrics tables, figures
outputs/                     December chart predictions
validation_predictions.csv   final predictions: load_id, predicted_rate
```

## How to run

Tested with Python 3.14 on Windows. From the repository root:

```
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate             # macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m pytest
python src/predict.py
```

`src/predict.py` trains the final model on all labelled loads (January-October), writes
`validation_predictions.csv` and `outputs/december_predictions.csv`, runs the provided
scorer on both files, and copies the scorer's December chart to
`reports/figures/6_candidate_december.png`. To run the scorer on its own:

```
python provided/score.py --predictions validation_predictions.csv --december-predictions outputs/december_predictions.csv
```

The other scripts reproduce the analysis: `python src/explore.py` (data facts, figures 1-4),
`python src/evaluate.py` (baseline metrics), `python src/compare.py` (model comparison,
figure 5) and `python src/report_to_docx.py` (Word version of the report).

## Outputs

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `validation_predictions.csv` | 12,000 predictions in the template's order, columns `load_id,predicted_rate` |
| `outputs/december_predictions.csv` | the 31 December chart rows with `predicted_rate` filled in; `data/` is left unchanged |
| `scorer_results/candidate_december.png` | the scorer's December chart, created when the scorer runs (not tracked in git) |
| `reports/figures/` | charts 1-6; the report uses 2, 5 and 6 |
| `reports/metrics_*.csv` | validation metrics for the baseline, the feature variants, the settings check and the quote_signal check |
| `reports/report.md`, `reports/report.docx` | write-up of the data, validation, model and December chart |

name: hos-trip-planner
description: Plan a truck trip under FMCSA hours-of-service rules and get the route, required stops and filled daily log sheets. Django + React.
content:
# hos-trip-planner

Plan a truck trip under FMCSA hours-of-service rules and get the route, required stops and filled daily log sheets. Django + React.

- 🔗 **Repository:** https://github.com/Mishallic/hos-trip-planner
- 🌐 **Website:** https://hos-trip-planner-web.vercel.app
- **Language:** Python
- **Topics:** django, eld, hours-of-service, react, trucking-service, typescript
- **Last update:** 2026-10-04

---

[![CI](https://github.com/Mishallic/hos-trip-planner/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Mishallic/hos-trip-planner/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

Plan a truck trip from the driver's current location, through the pickup, to the
drop-off. The planner places every stop the FMCSA hours-of-service rules require
(property-carrying driver, 70 hours / 8 days) and fills in the driver's daily log
sheets for every day of the trip.

**Live:** [hos-trip-planner-web.vercel.app](https://hos-trip-planner-web.vercel.app)

![The plan view: route map with every stop, the driver's clocks at the selected 10-hour rest, the stop list and the timeline](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mishallic/hos-trip-planner/main/docs/screenshot-map.png)

![A daily log sheet: the 24-hour grid with the duty line, line totals, remarks with brackets and flags, and the 70-hour recap](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mishallic/hos-trip-planner/main/docs/screenshot-log.png)

## What it does

**Inputs:** current location, pickup, drop-off, and the hours already used in the
70-hour cycle. Optional: start date and time (default now), the home terminal's time
zone, and the log header fields (driver, carrier, truck, trailer, shipper, commodity,
load number, home terminal). All inputs, and the view open, live in the URL, so a plan
is a shareable link and Back returns to the view before. Three sample trips on the empty
map plan in one click.

**Outputs:**
- **Route map** with the route and every stop: pre-trip inspections, pickup and
  drop-off, fuel, 30-minute breaks, 10-hour rests and 34-hour restarts.
- **Stop list** with the rule behind each stop ("11-hour driving limit reached after
  11:00 of driving").
- **Timeline** spaced by time, so a 34-hour restart reads as long.
- **Driver's clocks** (11-hour drive, 14-hour window, 8-hour break, 70-hour cycle)
  at any stop. The map, list, timeline and clocks share one selected stop.
- **Daily log sheets** drawn like the paper form (guide p. 15-19): header, the
  24-hour grid with the duty line at exact minutes, line totals adding to 24:00,
  remarks with a bracket and a 45° flag at every stop, and the 70-hour recap. One tab
  per day; "Print all days" gives one landscape page per day. A sheet that looks over a
  limit but is not (13 hours of driving across two duty periods) says why under it.
- **Turn-by-turn directions** with the stops in the order the driver reaches them.

## How the planner works

The engine (`backend/planner/domain/hos_engine.py`) is pure Python: no Django, no
HTTP, nothing outside the standard library (a test enforces this). Times are whole
minutes from the trip start; positions are miles along the route.

1. Drive as far as every clock allows: the 11-hour limit, the 14-hour window, the
   8-hour break rule, the 70-hour cycle, and the next fuel stop (at or before every
   1,000 miles).
2. Insert the stop the binding limit requires: a break, a 10-hour rest in the sleeper
   berth, a 34-hour restart, or fuel. Each stop records the limit that caused it.
3. Repeat until the drop-off. Pickup and drop-off are 1 hour on duty; every duty
   period that includes driving starts with a 30-minute pre-trip inspection.

The result is one timeline of events. Everything else is a view of it: the stops, the
clocks at each stop, and the daily logs (`log_builder.py`), which split the timeline
at midnight in the home terminal's time zone. How each minute of each duty status moves
the driver's clocks is written once (`DutyClocks` in `clocks.py`) and used by the engine,
the stop list and the recap; the tests check every plan against a separate statement of
the rules (`tests/hos_helpers.py`). The frontend draws; it contains no HOS logic.

Every limit and assumption is in one `HOSPolicy` object
(`backend/planner/domain/policy.py`). Where the rules leave room, the planner's
choices are listed below as D1-D19, and the code and tests cite them.

## Hours-of-service rules

The planner follows the FMCSA rules for a property-carrying driver on the
70-hour / 8-day schedule, as described in the FMCSA *Interstate Truck Driver's
Guide to Hours of Service* (April 2022). Code and tests cite it as "guide p. N".

| Rule | Limit | Guide |
|---|---|---|
| Driving limit | 11 hours of driving after 10 hours off duty | p. 6 |
| Driving window | no driving after the 14th hour since coming on duty | p. 6 |
| Break | 30 consecutive minutes off the wheel after 8 hours of cumulative driving | p. 10 |
| Cycle | no driving after 70 hours on duty in 8 days | p. 10-11 |
| Restart | 34 consecutive hours off duty resets the cycle | p. 11 |

### Planning decisions

Where the rules leave room, or the inputs don't say, the planner makes these
choices. Code and tests cite them as D1, D2, ...

…

name: weegood
description: Music that gets your vibe. Lightweight, local-first music player streaming real music with on-device learned recommendations.
content:
# weegood

Music that gets your vibe. Lightweight, local-first music player streaming real music with on-device learned recommendations.

- 🔗 **Repository:** https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood
- **Language:** TypeScript
- **Last update:** 2026-10-19

---

Music that gets your vibe.

Weegood is a lightweight, cross-platform music player that streams real, full-length music from
[Audius](https://audius.co), learns your taste on your own device, explains every recommendation,
and plays the files you already own alongside everything else.

**Status:** pre-alpha. The web app is feature complete on real music and ready for a tester round
(see [docs/ROADMAP.md](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/ROADMAP.md)). Mobile and desktop follow on the same core.

**Live:** https://mishallic.github.io/weegood/ , deployed from `main` on every push by GitHub Actions.

## What it does

- Streams real songs, full length, from an open music network. No account, no key, no licensing
  exposure for us. Every track links back to its artist on Audius.
- Learns your taste from a one-minute onboarding, then from every play, skip, like and follow,
  with a per-listener ranking model that trains on your device.
- Measures the audio of what you play, in your browser, to refine each track's vibe: loudness,
  brightness, bass, tempo, beat strength, key.
- Recommends tracks and artists with a plain-language reason attached to every pick.
- Lets you build playlists and follow artists, genres and people; what they repost and playlist
  feeds your home.
- Plays your own MP3, WAV, FLAC and OGG files next to streamed tracks, inside the same playlists.
- Keeps everything on your device. Nothing is sent anywhere but anonymous requests to the music
  network.

## Quickstart

Requires Node 24 (see `.node-version`). npm ships with Node, nothing else to install.

```sh
npm install
npm run dev        # web app on http://localhost:5173
npm test           # unit tests across all packages (offline)
npm run check      # typecheck + lint + format check (what CI runs)
npm run build      # production build of the web app
AUDIUS_LIVE=1 npx vitest run --project web src/providers/audius.live.test.ts   # hits the real API
```

## Repository layout

```
weegood/
├─ apps/
│  └─ web/              React + Vite web app: provider adapters, streaming engine, on-device analysis, UI
├─ packages/
│  └─ core/             Platform-agnostic domain, taxonomy, learned ranker, feature extraction (pure TypeScript)
├─ docs/
│  ├─ PRODUCT.md        Vision, personas, scope and success metrics
│  ├─ ARCHITECTURE.md   How the pieces fit together
│  ├─ ROADMAP.md        Milestones and prioritised TODOs
│  └─ adr/              Architecture Decision Records
└─ .github/workflows/   Continuous integration
```

## Principles

1. **Real music, honestly sourced.** Open networks and the listener's own accounts and files.
   Nothing scraped, nothing re-streamed against a service's terms.
2. **Lightweight by default.** Small bundle, system fonts, plain HTML5 audio for streaming.
3. **Local-first, privacy-first.** Taste profile, ranking model, playlists and files live on the
   device. Sync is an upgrade, not a requirement.
4. **Explainable recommendations.** The reason shown is the arithmetic that produced the score.
5. **One core, many shells.** Everything that is not pixels or platform APIs lives in
   `packages/core`.

## Documentation

Start with [docs/PRODUCT.md](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/PRODUCT.md), then [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md).
Decisions and their reasoning live in [docs/adr](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/adr); the two that matter most now are
[0010](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/adr/0010-real-music-from-streaming-providers.md) and
[0011](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/adr/0011-on-device-learned-ranking-and-audio-analysis.md). Open work lives in
[docs/ROADMAP.md](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/docs/ROADMAP.md). Contribution conventions are in [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Mishallic/weegood/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

name: daily-gallery
description: One artwork a day from public museum collections, with its story, materials, history and what critics wrote. Android app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
content:
# daily-gallery

One artwork a day from public museum collections, with its story, materials, history and what critics wrote. Android app in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.

- 🔗 **Repository:** https://github.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery
- **Language:** Kotlin
- **Last update:** 2026-10-16

---

[![CI](https://github.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

An Android app with one artwork a day from two public museum collections: the picture, the
story behind it, its materials and technique, its history (owners, exhibitions), what critics
and scholars wrote about it, and its artist. Earlier days stay in a gallery, and artworks you
save stay on the phone, ready to open offline.

![Today's artwork: the picture on a wall, its label, then the story, the owners on a dated timeline, and what critics wrote](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery/main/docs/screens-today.jpg)

![An earlier day opened from the gallery, the full-screen viewer, and today's page in the dark theme](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery/main/docs/screens-gallery.jpg)

## What it does

- **Today:** the day's artwork, hung on a wall: title, artist (with nationality and dates, or
  the culture for unattributed works), date, and tags (type, place, style). Share it, open it
  at the museum, or save it with the heart. A bar under the label jumps between the sections:
  - **The story:** the museum's own text, Cleveland's "Did you know?", then what Wikipedia says
    (background, description, subject, the work in popular culture).
  - **Materials & technique:** medium, materials, technique, support, dimensions,
    inscriptions, and conservation notes where the museum or Wikipedia has them.
  - **Through history:** the owners from the artist's studio to the museum, and the
    exhibitions it was shown in, on a timeline with years; Wikipedia's history of the work
    (acquisition, provenance, sales).
  - **What critics wrote:** Wikipedia's reception, interpretation and analysis of the work,
    what critics said about the artist, and the books and articles that discuss it, oldest
    first (117 for La Grande Jatte, starting with Jules Christophe's 1890 study of Seurat).
  - **About the artist**, and **Sources:** where the work is on view, its credit line and
    object number, and every source with its licence.
- **Gallery:** every day before today, newest first, as far back as the schedule goes without
  repeating. Each opens its own page.
- **Saved:** the artworks you saved, newest first, kept on the phone for offline reading.
- **Viewer:** tap the picture for it alone on black. Pinch or double-tap to zoom (up to 5x,
  in where you tapped); the sharper copy loads over the one on screen.

Everything shown is the museums' or Wikipedia's own text, and each passage names its source.
The app writes none of it.

## How it works

### The day's artwork

The schedule ships with the app: `app/src/main/assets/pool.json`, 472 artworks built by
[`scripts/build_pool.py`](https://github.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery/blob/main/scripts/build_pool.py) from

- the Art Institute of Chicago's 226 best-known public-domain works with a description (its
  "boosted" set), and
- the Cleveland Museum of Art's 246 CC0 highlights,

each linked through Wikidata to its English Wikipedia article (43 have one) and its artist's
(211). Day N after 16 October 2026 shows entry N, by the phone's local date, so every phone
shows the same artwork on the same day without a server; after the last entry the schedule
starts again. The order alternates the museums and keeps an artist at least two weeks apart.
A rebuild only appends, so a day that has been shown never changes.

### A day's page

`ArtworkRepository` reads the museum's record (and, for the Art Institute, the artist's) and
the Wikipedia articles on the work and the artist, side by side:

| Source | Gives |
| --- | --- |
| Museum record | title, artist, dates, image and its alt text, facts, the museum's text, owners, exhibitions, publications, the artist's biography |
| Wikipedia, the work | its sections, sorted by their headings into story, materials, history and critics; references and links are skipped |
| Wikipedia, the artist | what critics said (Legacy, Influence, Reception...), and the opening as a biography when the museum has none |

The museum is required; Wikipedia is not. When Wikipedia can't be reached the page shows
without it, says what is missing, and reads it again on the next visit. A finished artwork is
cached as JSON on the phone: it opens instantly and offline from then on. The cache keeps the 60
most recently opened artworks and every saved one. The label comes from the schedule, so it
shows at once even when nothing else can.

Some details the sources needed:

- Museum text is HTML (or plain text) with the titles of works in italics; it becomes
  paragraphs with the italics kept.
- The Art Institute's owners come as one sentence; they are split at semicolons outside
  brackets, and an owner's year is the last one outside brackets ("the artist's mother (died
  1899), Paris, 1891" is 1891).
- The Art Institute tags works with Getty vocabulary terms that repeat each other ("oil paint
  (paint)", "paint", "painting techniques"); only the specific ones are kept.
- Cleveland says when a work is only attributed ("Attributed to · Greek, Athenian"), and some
  of its "biographies" are only the artist's dates; those are not shown as one.

## Architecture

```
app/src/main/java/com/dailygallery/app/
  domain/   Pool (the schedule), Artwork, Text (museum HTML to paragraphs, years)   plain Kotlin
  data/     AicSource, ClevelandSource, WikipediaSource: one API each, mapped to an Artwork
            ArtworkRepository (puts a day together), ArtworkCache, SavedStore, OkHttpGet
  ui/       today/ (today, any day), artwork/ (the page and its sections), gallery/ (gallery,
            saved), viewer/ (zoom), theme/, AppNavigation (tabs and routes)
scripts/    build_pool.py (the schedule), dev.ps1 (emulator, tests, screen previews)
```

Kotlin and Jetpack Compose (Material 3), on the same toolchain as Job Watch (AGP 8.7, Kotlin
2.0, Gradle 8.10, JDK 17). OkHttp and kotlinx.serialization read the APIs, Coil 3 loads the
images, Navigation Compose joins the screens. Titles are set in
[Playfair Display](https://github.com/clauseggers/Playfair-Display) (SIL Open Font License,
[`licenses/OFL-PlayfairDisplay.txt`](https://github.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery/blob/main/licenses/OFL-PlayfairDisplay.txt)); running text in the
system sans.

## Tests

```powershell
.\gradlew testDebugUnitTest
```

72 tests, on the PC, with no device and no network:

- **Sources:** each API's saved responses (La Grande Jatte and Seurat from the Art Institute;
  The Red Kerchief, the Cleveland Apollo and a Chola bronze from Cleveland; three Wikipedia
  articles) mapped to an artwork, field by field.
- **Repository:** a day put together; read once and then from the cache; shown without
  Wikipedia and completed on the next visit; offline with and without a cached copy.
- **Schedule:** the day arithmetic, and the shipped pool (no repeats, both museums, https
  thumbnails, artists two weeks apart).
- **Text, zoom, HTTP client, saved list, cache pruning.**
- **Screens (Robolectric):** today's page and every section, offline, without Wikipedia, the
  dark theme, the viewer, the gallery, a past day, saving and unsaving, and the app starting.
  They run on saved responses and the real images, and draw each screen to
  `app/build/screenshots`.

A live check reads the first 30 days of the schedule from the real museums and Wikipedia and
fetches every image. It is off by default; run it after rebuilding the pool:

```powershell
$env:DAILY_GALLERY_LIVE = "1"; .\gradlew testDebugUnitTest --tests "*LiveSourcesTest" --rerun
```

**CI** (GitHub Actions) runs lint, the tests and the build on every push, and keeps the drawn
screens as an artifact.

## Limits

…

[Read the full README on GitHub](https://github.com/Mishallic/daily-gallery#readme)

name: linkedin-job-fetcher
description: Watches LinkedIn job searches every 10 minutes and alerts you about new jobs: Android app, Windows desktop app and iPhone script.
content:
# linkedin-job-fetcher

Watches LinkedIn job searches every 10 minutes and alerts you about new jobs: Android app, Windows desktop app and iPhone script.

- 🔗 **Repository:** https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher
- **Language:** Kotlin
- **Last update:** 2026-10-19

---

[![Android](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/actions/workflows/android.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/actions/workflows/android.yml)

Watches your LinkedIn job searches and tells you about new and reposted jobs soon after
they're posted. It uses LinkedIn's public, logged-out job search, so it needs no LinkedIn
account or API key.

There are three versions of it:

| Version | Where it runs | How it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Job Watch** ([`android/`](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/blob/main/android)) | Android phone: each LinkedIn search every 5 minutes, plus remote job boards and job sites | Phone notification, plus optional email and WhatsApp |
| **Desktop app** (`jobs_ui.py`) | Windows PC, while the window is open | Email and WhatsApp; a phone page over Wi-Fi |
| **iPhone script** ([`iphone/Jobs.js`](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/blob/main/iphone/Jobs.js)) | iPhone, in the free Scriptable app, when iOS allows | iPhone notification, plus optional WhatsApp |

Each check reads every page of results posted since the previous check (plus a 5-minute
overlap), so a late or skipped check doesn't miss jobs. Jobs you've already been told about
are never repeated.

## Android app (Job Watch)

**Install:** download `JobWatch-.apk` from this repository's
[Releases](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/blob/main/../../releases) on the phone, open it, and allow installing from that source.
On first launch, allow notifications and tap **Allow** on the "Finish setting up" card so
Android doesn't pause the checks. The **Check every 5 minutes** switch turns background
checks off and on.

**How often LinkedIn is asked:** one search a minute at most, whatever starts the check:
the alarm, the refresh button or a new search. Each search's turn comes 5 minutes after
its last one, so with 5 searches, the most Job Watch takes, LinkedIn gets 5 requests every
5 minutes rather than a burst of them; with fewer, the app sleeps until the next turn.
A search with more new jobs than one page holds reads one page per turn. If LinkedIn asks to
slow down, background checks leave it alone for 10 minutes; the refresh button can try again
after a minute. The phone is told about new jobs by the check that finds them; email and WhatsApp
go at most every 10 minutes, all together, or at once for a check you ask for. Opening the app
doesn't check again; the refresh button checks the next search at once, or says when it goes.

**Recent checks**, under the switch, lists the last 100 checks: when each started, what
started it (the alarm, the refresh button, a new search, opening the app), how long it took
and what it found. A check the phone stopped before it finished shows as such, and so does
one the phone ran a minute or more late.

**Delivery times**, next to it, shows how long the last day's LinkedIn jobs took from being
posted to being found, and from being found to the notification: the median and the time 9 in
10 jobs were within, and each job's own times. **Share** sends it all as text. How these
measures were used to find why jobs came late is written up in
[docs/investigations/2026-10-19-late-notifications.md](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/blob/main/docs/investigations/2026-10-19-late-notifications.md).

**New, read and deleted:** a filled dot marks a new job, an empty circle a read one. Tap the
dot to switch it, or open the job to mark it read. Long-press a job to select several, then
**Mark as read**, **Mark as new** or **Select all** from the bar at the bottom, or the trash
button to delete them (with **Undo** for a few seconds). Deleted jobs don't come back.

**Remote job boards:** besides LinkedIn, Job Watch reads the official feeds of We Work
Remotely, Himalayas, Remote OK, Jobicy and Remotive, and the posts in Hacker News's monthly
"Who is hiring?" thread (through its official search API). It keeps jobs whose title contains one
of your positions and that are open worldwide or to the places in your searches (or to
EMEA, the Middle East or the GCC). These boards ask apps to link to the original listing
and name them as the source, so every job shows which board it came from. The boards are
read on the same checks as LinkedIn, each only as often as its terms allow:

| Board | Read |
| --- | --- |
| We Work Remotely, Himalayas, Remote OK | every 10 minutes (no limit) |
| Jobicy | hourly (its limit) |
| Hacker News | hourly, only the posts since the last read |
| Remotive | every 6 hours (its limit: 4 times a day) |

On mobile data every board is read at most hourly: reading them all downloads about 400 KB,
which every 10 minutes would come to about 60 MB a day.

**Job sites:** ReliefWeb (run by the UN's humanitarian office, OCHA) and Jooble (a job search
engine) look for your positions in the places of your searches, through their official feed
and API, and their jobs show under the search they match. ReliefWeb needs no key; it lists UN
and NGO jobs, few of them in software or data, and asks feed readers to wait an hour between
reads. Jooble covers the UAE and Saudi Arabia but not Jordan, and needs a free API key: get
one at [jooble.org/api/about](https://jooble.org/api/about) (its form asks for a website) and
paste it into the **Job sites** card. Each is read at most hourly, Jooble one search per hour
each. A job already found on LinkedIn isn't announced again from a job site.

**Build** (JDK 17 and the Android SDK with platform 35):

```
cd android
./gradlew assembleRelease        # app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk
./gradlew testReleaseUnitTest    # unit, simulation and Robolectric UI tests; no network needed
```

`local.properties` (git-ignored) must point at the SDK: `sdk.dir=C\:\\path\\to\\Android\\Sdk`.
GitHub Actions runs the same tests and the release build on every push and pull request.
`LIVE_LINKEDIN=1 ./gradlew testReleaseUnitTest --tests "*liveFetchFromLinkedIn"` checks, with one
real request, that LinkedIn's results page still reads.
Release builds are signed with the building machine's debug key, so an update installs over
an earlier version only when both were built on the same machine.

## Desktop app

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
python jobs_ui.py                                    # window with searches, jobs and alerts
python linkedin_jobs.py -k "data analyst" -l "Dubai" # or a single search in the console
```

Email uses SMTP (for Gmail, an App Password); WhatsApp uses the free CallMeBot service.
The files it writes while running (`settings.json`, `searches.json`, `jobs.csv`, and so on)
hold passwords and personal data and are kept out of git.

## iPhone script

Copy [`iphone/Jobs.js`](https://github.com/Mishallic/linkedin-job-fetcher/blob/main/iphone/Jobs.js) into a new script in the Scriptable app and run it
once. Background checks come from a Scriptable home-screen widget or a Shortcuts automation;
iOS decides how often those run.

## Good to know

- LinkedIn limits how often one internet connection can use its job search (HTTP 429).
  Job Watch asks for one search a minute at most, and after a refusal leaves LinkedIn
  alone for 10 minutes. The desktop app and the iPhone script stop the current round after one
  request and try again at the next check.
- Use "City, Country" for locations. "Jordan" on its own is read by LinkedIn as Danville, PA,
  so use "Amman, Jordan".
- LinkedIn's terms don't allow automated scraping. This is meant for light personal use.

# personal-website

My personal website

- 🔗 **Repository:** https://github.com/Mishallic/personal-website
- 🌐 **Website:** https://personal-website-blue-nu-23.vercel.app
- **Language:** JavaScript
- **Last update:** 2026-10-19

---

A portfolio with a terminal interface. Type `help` in the prompt to see the commands.

- `frontend/` React (Create React App) + Redux Toolkit. The CLI, the command processor and the markdown reader.
- `backend/` Express + MySQL. Serves `/projects`, `/blogs` and `/log`.
- `api/` + `vercel.json` Vercel deployment: static frontend plus the backend as a serverless function.

## Run locally

**Full stack with Docker Compose** (frontend on :3000, API on :8000, MySQL on :3308, adminer on :8080):

```sh
cp env_file_example env_file                 # MySQL credentials
cp backend/.example.env backend/.env         # API settings, DB_HOST=mysql inside compose
docker compose -f docker-compose.local.yml up --build
```

**Frontend only** (no database: projects and blog stay empty):

```sh
cd frontend && npm install && npm start
```

**Backend only** against an existing MySQL:

```sh
cd backend && npm install && cp .example.env .env   # edit DB_* in .env
npm start
```

Tests: `cd frontend && CI=true npm test`.

## Deploy on Vercel

The repo root is the Vercel project root. `vercel.json` builds `frontend/` into a static site and
exposes `backend/app.js` through `api/index.js`; rewrites map `/projects`, `/blogs` and `/log` to it.

1. Import the repository on vercel.com, or run `vercel` in the repo root.
2. Add the environment variables from `backend/.example.env` to the project
   (`DB_HOST`, `DB_PORT`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`, `DB_DATABASE`), pointing at a MySQL instance
   reachable from Vercel. Without them the site still deploys, and the API answers 500 for
   database-backed routes.
3. Deploy. Production deployments build from `main`.
